record.reason: Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b) is the governing ground for the petition and directly supplies the elements of post-9 June 1952 subletting, assignment or parting with possession without written landlord consent. The supplied record squarely disputes both possession/identity and the claimed consent.
record.law_quote: sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord

record.reason: This is the Andhra Pradesh rent statute, not the Delhi provision governing the fixed ground, and the supplied record contains no Andhra Pradesh tenancy issue. Because Delhi section 14(1)(b) is separately supplied, this statutory unit does not help resolve the live Delhi question.
record.law_quote: without the written consent of the landlord

record.reason: The Supreme Court application concerns a court-sanctioned amalgamation under the Andhra Pradesh Act where the original tenant company dissolved and its lease rights vested in a transferee. Here the record shows only that the tenant firm's two partners were also directors of a separately incorporated company, with no amalgamation or statutory vesting shown, so the authority is a qualified contrast rather than decisive law.
record.law_quote: the 1st appellant company is no longer in existence in the eye of law

record.reason: The Supreme Court's report of Parasaram directly states the breadth of Delhi section 14(b), including assignment and other modes of parting and even an involuntary sale. That materially bears on the petitioner's alternative assignment/parting theory, although the reported liquidation-sale setting is factually different.
record.law_quote: the amplitude of S. 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was wide enough not only to include any sublease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted

record.reason: This unit concerns Bombay Rent Act section 15A protected-licensee status and an Esso acquisition setting. The supplied Delhi record presents no protected-licensee claim, Bombay statutory issue or comparable acquisition mechanism, so it is out of scope for the fixed section 14(1)(b) question.
record.law_quote: status of deemed tenant or protected licensee under s. 15A of the Bombay Rent Act

record.reason: The authority addresses specific statutory vesting under the Esso Acquisition Act, related notification and Companies Act section 396 in a Bombay Rent Act setting. No acquisition, statutory vesting or comparable scheme appears in the supplied record.
record.law_quote: the right, title and interest of Esso Eastern In6. in relation to its undertakings in India, shall stand transferred to, and sh~ll vest in, the Central Government

record.reason: The Delhi High Court passage provides company-amalgamation context but expressly reserves whether a court-ordered amalgamation amounts to an assignment attracting section 14(1)(b). The present record alleges incorporation and occupation by another company, not an amalgamation, so the passage is only a qualified analogy.
record.law_quote: This court is, however, not concerned at this stage if the transfer by or consequent on amalgamation by the order of the court would nevertheless be tantamount to the assignment of a tenancy

record.reason: Banking Regulation Act section 44A governs amalgamation of banking companies. Neither the tenant nor the alleged occupant is a banking company and no banking amalgamation is part of the supplied record.
record.law_quote: Procedure for amalgamation of banking companies

record.reason: Banking Regulation Act section 45 concerns RBI/Central Government reconstruction or amalgamation of banking companies. The supplied parties and alleged occupation involve a partnership firm and a private company, not a bank or an RBI scheme.
record.law_quote: the Reserve Bank may prepare a scheme

record.reason: This 1980 banking-acquisition provision concerns Central Government schemes for corresponding new banks. No corresponding new bank, nationalised-bank scheme or statutory banking transfer appears in the record.
record.law_quote: The Central Govemment may, after consultation with the Reserve Banl<, make a scheme

record.reason: The New Bank of India scheme specifically transfers that bank's undertaking to Punjab National Bank. It has no factual connection to the tenant partnership, M/s Anil & Co. Pvt. Ltd., or the alleged parting with possession in this Delhi shop.
record.law_quote: Undertaking of New Bank of India to vest in Punjab National Bank

record.reason: Delhi section 16 directly supplements section 14(1)(b): post-9 June 1952 subletting without written consent is not lawful, and post-commencement transfer or assignment requires previous written landlord consent. The respondent's alleged 1964 permission and the later company use from 1997 make the existence and scope of written consent a live issue.
record.law_quote: no tenant shall, without the previous consent in writing of the landlord

record.reason: Section 17 provides procedural context for a subtenancy created with previous written consent and notice to the landlord. No supplied segment identifies a section 17 notice or an independent protected-subtenant claim, so it is meaningful context but not decisive of the fixed section 14(1)(b) ground.
record.law_quote: with the previous consent in writing of the landlord

record.reason: Section 18 governs when a protected subtenant becomes a direct tenant after an eviction order or termination of the head tenancy. The fixed task is whether the section 14(1)(b) ground is made out, and no section 18 protection claim appears in the supplied record.
record.law_quote: the sub-tenant shall, with effect from the date of the order, be deemed to become a tenant holding directly under the landlord

record.reason: Delhi section 14(4) targets a sham business partnership where a person is ostensibly admitted as a partner but is really a subtenant. Here the alleged occupant is a private company whose directors overlap with the tenant firm's partners, not a person alleged to be an ostensible partner of the tenant, so the provision is a useful limiting analogy rather than directly triggered.
record.law_quote: ostensibly on the ground that such person is a partner of the tenant in the business or profession but really for the purpose of sub-letting such premises to that person

record.reason: The Supreme Court cautions that family occupation or permissive use does not by itself justify an inference of subletting. The overlap here is between spouses who are both partners of the tenant firm and directors of a private company, so the family-use principle is relevant only by analogy and cannot resolve the separate-corporate-occupation issue.
record.law_quote: it will be in the absence of any other evidence, a rash inference to draw that the owner has let out that part of the premises

record.reason: This Delhi authority clarifies that section 14(4) requires an ostensible partnership masking real subletting and is not a presumption applicable to every family or business occupation. It constrains any partnership-based inference here, but the alleged occupant is a company rather than an ostensible partner of the tenant.
record.law_quote: the premises could be deemed to have been sub-let by the tenant only when the Controller is satisfied that some person is let into possession ostensibly as a partner in business but really for the purposes of sub-letting

record.reason: This Supreme Court Delhi rule places the initial burden of proving subletting on the landlord and identifies exclusive possession for valuable consideration as a basis for shifting the evidentiary burden. The petitioner's submission expressly claims that Anil & Co.'s admitted operation from the premises discharged that initial onus, while the respondent disputes exclusive independent possession.
record.law_quote: the onus to prove sub-letting is on the landlord

record.reason: The Supreme Court synthesis states that introducing partners does not by itself amount to subletting and that a tenant who remains actively associated and retains control may not have parted with possession. That directly bears on the respondent's claim that the same two people remain partners of the tenant firm and directors operating the company, although the source statute was Goa law and the principle is analogical here.
record.law_quote: If tenant is actively associated with the partnership business and retains the control over the tenancy premises with him, may be along with partners, the tenant may not be said to have parted with possession.

record.reason: This passage allows a court to look behind an ostensible partnership and examine whether a formal arrangement conceals real subletting. The record contains partnership deeds and evidence of a separate company, but no supplied finding that the partnership is sham or that pleading variance caused no prejudice, so the passage is only an evidentiary analogy.
record.law_quote: the court may be required to tear the veil of partnership to find out the real nature of transaction entered into by the tenant

record.reason: The petitioner expressly invoked Celina Coelho Pereira and argued for a presumption once a third party was shown operating from the premises. The supplied synthesis directly structures the inquiry into exclusive possession, retained legal possession and burden shifting, while its Goa-statute formulation about consideration should not be mechanically extended to every Delhi assignment or parting alternative.
record.law_quote: initial burden lying on landlord would stand discharged by adducing prima facie proof of the fact that a party other than tenant was in exclusive possession of the premises

record.reason: The Bombay authority emphasizes that genuine partnership depends on real intention and agency, and that allowing another to use premises does not create a sublease if the lessee retains legal possession. That is useful to assess the respondent's partnership-and-control narrative, but the governing statute differs and the present dispute also involves a separate private company.
record.law_quote: The mere fact that another is allowed to use the premises while the lessee retains the legal possession is not enough to create a sub-lease.

record.reason: This older Delhi-and-Ajmer authority treats exclusive possession as an important but nonconclusive indicator and focuses on retained control when distinguishing a lease from a licence. Exclusive independent possession is disputed here, but no written grant between the tenant firm and Anil & Co. is supplied, making the passage a qualified evidentiary analogy rather than decisive 1958 Act law.
record.law_quote: The test of exclusive possession, though not conclusive, is a very important indication in favour of tenancy

record.reason: The older Act case supports an inference from exclusive possession for valuable consideration where the occupant's written agreements were withheld. In the supplied record, exclusive possession is disputed and no consideration or withheld occupancy agreement between the respondent and Anil & Co. is identified, so the burden principle is relevant but not decisive.
record.law_quote: The respondent discharged the onus by leading evidence showing that the occupants were in exclusive possession of the apartments for valuable consideration.

record.reason: The authority is materially useful to the respondent's claimed 1964 permission because it rejects treating a general lease purpose or earlier correspondence as blanket consent to later sublettings and stresses written consent tied to the relevant letting. Although it interprets the 1952 Delhi-and-Ajmer Act, it directly frames whether an alleged family/business permission could cover Anil & Co.'s later occupation from 1997.
record.law_quote: it is impossible to read in cl. 22 an implied consent to sub-letting

record.reason: This Supreme Court Delhi case shows that where one company actually assigns its leasehold to another, continuing the same business and a regulatory background do not eliminate the written-consent requirement. The present record supplies no assignment agreement or FERA-style transfer, so it is a useful corporate contrast rather than a direct match.
record.law_quote: it is a case of assignment of the leasehold right, had from the respondent in favour of India Company

record.reason: This Supreme Court Delhi passage, quoting Parasaram, confirms that section 14(1)(b) reaches assignment and other modes of parting and is not confined to consensual subleases. It materially bears on the petitioner's alternative assignment/parting theory and its argument about succession after Dina Nath Kapur's death, while the liquidation-sale facts remain distinct.
record.law_quote: The language of s.14(b) is wide enough not only to include any sub- lease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted.

record.reason: The Supreme Court's Delhi sections 17-18 discussion explains that consent to a particular subtenancy must be evidenced in writing and clearly indicate the landlord's consent and knowledge. That materially helps assess the respondent's alleged 1964 permission for later corporate occupation, though the passage concerns subtenant protection rather than section 14(1)(b) itself.
record.law_quote: The writing is to be such as to indicate clearly the consent of the landlord to the creation of a sub-tenancy

record.reason: The concurrence cautions that a landlord's signature on some tenancy communication should not generally be treated as satisfying the written-consent conditions and labels its own result exceptional. This is useful limiting context to the supplied consent authority, but it is a concurrence focused on sections 17-18 rather than a direct section 14(1)(b) holding.
record.law_quote: This, according to me, is an exceptional case with facts peculiar to its own.

record.reason: The Supreme Court directly states that Delhi commercial tenancies devolve on heirs under ordinary succession, which materially counters the proposition that post-death succession itself necessarily amounts to parting with possession. The record says Dina Nath Kapur's sons took over after his death under a Will, so the authority is central but does not itself resolve the distinct effect of a testamentary devise rather than ordinary inheritance.
record.law_quote: commercial tenancies notwithstanding the determination of the contractual tenancies will devolve on the heirs in accordance with law
